blocks.text: 1. Introduction

Think about how you find someone in your phone. If you know their name, you type "Alice" into search and jump straight to her contact. That is selecting by label. But sometimes you just want "the fifth contact I added," regardless of what their name is. That is selecting by position. Pandas gives you one tool for each of these jobs, and mixing them up is one of the most common sources of bugs and confusing warnings for people new to pandas.

You have already seen glimpses of .loc and .iloc in the Series and DataFrame lessons. This lesson is where you get the full picture: what each one actually does under the hood, the slicing behavior that catches almost everyone off guard at least once, how to select a mix of rows and columns with either tool, how boolean masking plugs into .loc, and a nasty little trap called the SettingWithCopyWarning that you will eventually run into if you write pandas code long enough.

blocks.alt: A DataFrame branching into loc which selects by label and iloc which selects by position
blocks.caption: Two tools, two completely different ways of pointing at the same data.

blocks.text: Every example below uses the same small DataFrame: five employees, indexed by their name, with columns for department, salary, and years of experience. Keeping one running example makes it much easier to see exactly what changes between .loc and .iloc.

code.content:
import pandas as pd

data = {
    "department": ["Engineering", "Marketing", "Engineering", "Sales", "Marketing"],
    "salary":     [95000, 68000, 105000, 72000, 71000],
    "years":      [3, 5, 8, 2, 4],
}
df = pd.DataFrame(data, index=["alice", "bob", "carol", "dave", "eve"])
print(df)

blocks.title: Two different worlds
blocks.content: Notice the DataFrame has both meaningful row labels, the employee names, and an implicit position for every row, 0 through 4. loc lives in the label world. iloc lives in the position world. They will often give you the exact same row, but they get there in completely different ways, and that difference matters a lot once you start slicing.

blocks.text: 2. .loc: Selecting by Label

.loc selects rows and columns using their actual labels, the names that show up in the index and in the column headers. It does not care what position something sits at. If you ask for "carol", you get whichever row is labeled carol, no matter where it physically lives in the DataFrame.
2.1 Selecting a Single Row or Cell by Label
Pass a single label to get that whole row back as a Series, with the column names becoming the new index.

code.content:
row = df.loc["alice"]
print(row)
# department    Engineering
# salary              95000
# years                   3
# Name: alice, dtype: object

blocks.text: To reach a single cell, pass both the row label and the column label, row first, then column, separated by a comma.

blocks.title: Always row, then column
blocks.content: This order never flips. df.loc[row_selector, column_selector]. If you only give one value, pandas assumes you meant the row selector and returns every column for that row.

blocks.text: 2.2 Slicing With .loc Is Inclusive of the End Label
Here is the part that trips up almost everyone the first time. You can slice by label using the same colon syntax you already know from Python lists.

In a normal Python list, my_list[0:2] stops before index 2, it never touches it. But df.loc["alice":"carol"] gives you alice, bob, AND carol. The end label is included, not excluded. This is genuinely different behavior from every other slicing you have used in Python so far, and it is not a bug, it is intentional pandas design, because label slicing needs to feel natural for things like date ranges, where you would expect "January 1 through January 31" to actually include January 31.

blocks.alt: A chain of four labels, alice, bob, carol, dave, with alice through carol highlighted green to show the slice includes the end label
blocks.caption: loc slicing from alice to carol keeps carol too. The end label is part of the result.

blocks.title: Inclusive end, and it is on purpose
blocks.content: df.loc["alice":"carol"] includes carol. Compare that to a plain Python list, where list[0:2] would stop before position 2. Label based slicing in pandas is deliberately inclusive on both ends because labels do not have a reliable "next one after this" the way integer positions do.

blocks.text: This inclusive behavior applies to columns too. df.loc[:, "department":"salary"] keeps every column from department through salary, salary included.
2.3 Selecting a Mix of Specific Rows and Columns
Instead of a single label or a slice, you can pass a plain list of labels. This is how you pick out an arbitrary, non contiguous handful of rows.

blocks.alt: loc branching out to three specific rows, alice, carol, and eve, picked from a list of labels
blocks.caption: A list of labels lets you cherry pick rows that are not next to each other in the DataFrame.

blocks.text: The same trick works for columns, and you can combine a row list with a column list to pull out exactly the rectangle of data you want.

code.content:
chunk = df.loc[["alice", "carol"], ["department", "years"]]
print(chunk)
#        department  years
# alice  Engineering      3
# carol  Engineering      8

blocks.text: 2.4 Boolean Selection With .loc

You already met boolean masking back in the NumPy module: an array of True and False values, one per element, used to filter data. Pandas Series support that exact same trick, and .loc is the natural place to plug a boolean mask in, because a mask is really just another way of picking out rows, not by name and not by position, but by whether a condition holds.

code.content:
mask = df["salary"] > 70000
print(mask.tolist())
# [True, False, True, True, True]

high_earners = df.loc[mask]
print(high_earners.index.tolist())
# ["alice", "carol", "dave", "eve"]

blocks.text: You can also skip the intermediate variable and write the condition directly inside .loc, and you can pair it with a column selector in the same call, exactly like the row label plus column label pattern from earlier.

code.content:
departments_of_high_earners = df.loc[df["salary"] > 70000, "department"]
print(departments_of_high_earners)
# alice    Engineering
# carol    Engineering
# dave          Sales
# eve       Marketing
# Name: department, dtype: object

blocks.alt: A salary condition producing a boolean mask, which then feeds into loc alongside a column selector
blocks.caption: A boolean mask is just another kind of selector that loc knows how to use.

blocks.title: This connects straight back to NumPy
blocks.content: Under the hood, that True and False array works the same way boolean masks worked on plain NumPy arrays. Pandas just extends the idea so it lines up with row labels, and lets loc use it as a first class selector.

blocks.text: 3. .iloc: Selecting by Position

.iloc ignores labels completely. It only cares about pure integer position, counting from 0, exactly like a plain Python list or a NumPy array. Row 0 is whatever the first row happens to be, regardless of whether its label is "alice", "2024-01-01", or anything else.
3.1 Selecting a Single Row or Cell by Position
Pass a single integer to get that row back as a Series.

code.content:
row = df.iloc[0]
print(row.name)   # "alice", the label of the row sitting at position 0

blocks.text: For a single cell, give the row position and the column position, in that order, same comma pattern as loc.

code.content:
value = df.iloc[2, 1]
print(value)   # 105000, row position 2 is carol, column position 1 is salary

blocks.title: Position, not label, all the way through
blocks.content: df.iloc[2, 1] has nothing to do with the label carol or the column name salary. It only means "third row, second column", counting from zero. It just happens that the third row is carol in this particular DataFrame.

blocks.text: 3.2 Slicing With .iloc Is Exclusive of the End Position

Now for the part that makes iloc feel familiar and predictable in exactly the way loc slicing did not. iloc slices work precisely like slicing a normal Python list or a NumPy array: the end position is excluded.

code.content:
subset = df.iloc[0:2]
print(subset.index.tolist())
# ["alice", "bob"]     position 2, carol, is NOT included

blocks.alt: A chain of four positions, 0, 1, 2, 3, with positions 0 and 1 highlighted blue as included and 2 and 3 shown grey as excluded
blocks.caption: iloc slicing from position 0 to 2 stops before position 2, standard Python slicing rules.

blocks.title: Exclusive end, same as any Python list
blocks.content: df.iloc[0:2] gives you positions 0 and 1 only. Position 2 is the stopping point, not part of the result. This is the ordinary slicing rule you already know from lists and NumPy arrays. iloc never surprises you here, loc does.

blocks.text: Put the two side by side and the contrast becomes very easy to remember.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Call","Rows returned","End included"],"rows":[["df.loc[\"alice\":\"carol\"]","alice, bob, carol","Yes"],["df.iloc[0:2]","alice, bob","No"],["df.iloc[0:3]","alice, bob, carol","No, position 3 would be dave"]]}

blocks.text: 3.3 Selecting a Mix of Specific Rows and Columns
Exactly like loc, you can pass a list of positions instead of a single integer or a slice, to grab a non contiguous set of rows.

code.content:
picked = df.iloc[[0, 2, 4]]
print(picked.index.tolist())
# ["alice", "carol", "eve"]     same three rows as the loc list example earlier

blocks.alt: iloc branching out to three specific positions, 0, 2, and 4, picked from a list of integer positions
blocks.caption: A list of positions works just like a list of labels does with loc, just counted differently.

blocks.text: And you can combine a row position list with a column position list to select a specific rectangle.

code.content:
chunk = df.iloc[[0, 2], [0, 2]]
print(chunk)
#        department  years
# alice  Engineering      3
# carol  Engineering      8

blocks.text: 4. loc vs iloc: When to Use Which
4.1 The Simple Rule
Ask yourself one question: do you know the specific, meaningful label you want, or do you just want "the Nth one" regardless of what it is called?

items: You know a specific date, an ID, or a name you care about, like a stock price on "2024-03-15" or the row for customer "CUST-4471". Reach for loc.
You want the first row, the last five rows, or "everything from row 10 onward" without caring what their labels happen to be. Reach for iloc.

blocks.alt: A decision diamond asking whether you know the exact label, branching to loc for yes and iloc for no
blocks.caption: When in doubt, ask whether the label itself matters to what you are doing.

blocks.text: A useful habit: if your code has a literal string or a literal date sitting inside the brackets, that is a strong sign you want loc. If your code has a plain integer that represents "how many rows in" rather than a real identifier, that is a sign you want iloc.
4.2 Full Comparison

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect",".loc",".iloc"],"rows":[["Selects by","label / index name","integer position"],["Slice end","included","excluded, standard Python rule"],["Accepts a boolean mask","yes","not directly, needs .to_numpy or similar"],["Order matters if labels change","no, follows the label wherever it sits","yes, follows raw position only"],["Typical use case","a known date, ID, or name","the Nth row, a fixed size window"],["Example","df.loc[\"alice\":\"carol\"]","df.iloc[0:2]"]]}

blocks.alt: A small reference diagram summarizing loc as label based with inclusive slice ends and iloc as position based with exclusive slice ends
blocks.caption: The two headline differences to keep in your head at all times.

blocks.title: One more wrinkle worth knowing
blocks.content: If your DataFrame index happens to be plain integers, like the default 0, 1, 2 pandas gives you automatically, loc and iloc can look confusingly similar. df.loc[0:2] would then still be inclusive and give you three rows, while df.iloc[0:2] gives you two. Same looking numbers, different rules, because loc is still reading them as labels, not positions.

blocks.text: 5. The Chained Indexing Trap: SettingWithCopyWarning
5.1 Why Chained Indexing Is Ambiguous
Here is a pattern that looks completely reasonable and will eventually bite you: filtering a DataFrame with square brackets, then immediately trying to assign into a column of the result.

code.content:
# The trap. Do not write assignments like this.
df[df["salary"] > 70000]["years"] = 0

# Pandas prints something like:
# SettingWithCopyWarning: A value is trying to be set on a copy of a slice from a DataFrame

blocks.text: This is called chained indexing because you are chaining two separate bracket operations back to back: first df[df["salary"] > 70000], which produces some in between object, and then ["years"] = 0 on top of that in between object. The problem is that pandas cannot always tell you, in advance, whether that first step handed you back a genuine view into the original DataFrame or an independent copy of it. Sometimes it is one, sometimes the other, depending on the internal layout of the data, and it can change between pandas versions.

blocks.alt: A filtered DataFrame producing an intermediate object that could ambiguously be either a view or a copy, both marked red
blocks.caption: The intermediate object from the first set of brackets is the ambiguous part. Pandas genuinely does not always know what it is.

blocks.text: If that in between object is a view, your assignment actually changes the original df, which is what you probably wanted. If it is a copy, your assignment changes a throwaway object that gets discarded immediately, and df is left completely untouched, silently. That silent failure is exactly why pandas raises the warning: it wants to tell you "I am not confident this assignment did what you think it did."

blocks.title: The warning is a symptom, not the disease
blocks.content: SettingWithCopyWarning does not mean your code crashed. It means pandas found a spot where the intent of your code is ambiguous. Sometimes the assignment quietly works anyway, sometimes it quietly does nothing. Either way, do not just ignore the warning and hope for the best.

blocks.text: 5.2 The Fix: One Single .loc Call

The fix is simple once you see it: never chain two separate bracket operations when you intend to assign. Instead, express the row condition and the column you want to touch inside one single .loc call.

code.content:
# The fix. One loc call does both the filtering and the assignment.
df.loc[df["salary"] > 70000, "years"] = 0

print(df)
#        department  salary  years
# alice  Engineering   95000      0
# bob      Marketing   68000      5
# carol  Engineering  105000      0
# dave         Sales   72000      0
# eve      Marketing   71000      0

blocks.text: Because everything happens inside one call, pandas always knows exactly which rows and which column you mean, and it can guarantee the assignment lands directly on the original df. There is no ambiguous in between object for it to worry about, so there is no warning, and no silent no op.

blocks.alt: A condition feeding into a single loc call that updates the DataFrame directly, both marked green
blocks.caption: One loc call, one clear target. No ambiguity, no warning.

blocks.title: The rule of thumb to keep for life
blocks.content: Reading data back out, df[df["salary"] > 70000]["years"] is a bit sloppy but usually harmless. Assigning into data, that exact same pattern is a trap. Whenever you are writing a value, not just reading one, use a single df.loc[row_condition, column] = value call and this warning simply never shows up.

blocks.text: 6. Wrapping Up

loc and iloc solve the same underlying problem, picking rows and columns out of a DataFrame, from two different angles. loc speaks the language of labels: names, dates, IDs, anything meaningful to you. iloc speaks the language of raw position: 0, 1, 2, exactly like a Python list. Once you have that split clear in your head, the slicing behavior, the list selection, and the boolean masking all fall into place as natural consequences of which world each tool lives in.

blocks.alt: A selection request splitting into a list of row labels and a list of column labels, both feeding into a resulting subset
blocks.caption: Whether you are using loc or iloc, mixing a row selector with a column selector is how you carve out exactly the piece of data you need.

items: loc selects by label. Slices are inclusive of the end label, a genuine exception to normal Python slicing rules.
iloc selects by pure integer position. Slices are exclusive of the end position, the same rule every Python list already follows.
Both accept a single value, a slice, or a list, for rows and for columns, and you can mix row and column selectors in one call.
loc also accepts a boolean mask directly, the same idea as boolean masking on NumPy arrays, letting you filter rows by a condition.
Never chain two separate bracket operations when assigning a value. Use one single loc call, df.loc[condition, column] = value, to avoid the SettingWithCopyWarning entirely.

blocks.title: Where this goes next
blocks.content: Selecting the right slice of data is step one. The next lessons build on exactly this foundation: grouping rows together, reshaping tables, and combining multiple DataFrames, all of which lean on the same loc and iloc habits you just built here.
